cues.text: Section eleven.
Practical lab: cloud FinOps.
Let us work through a practical exercise.
FinTechNova faces a four hundred percent increase in its cloud bill.
The exercise identifies instances with average CPU utilisation below ten percent as candidates for investigation.
First, look at the inventory table.
It has four columns: Instance, Department, Monthly cost, and CPU.
Take it row by row.
The first row is instance i-0a1b2c, owned by Marketing, costing four hundred and fifty dollars a month, with CPU at eighty-five percent.
The second row is instance i-9x8y7z, in Development, costing nine hundred dollars a month, with CPU at four point five percent.
The third row is instance i-5m6n7o, in Core Banking, costing one thousand five hundred dollars a month, with CPU at sixty percent.
The fourth row is instance i-1q2w3e, also in Development, costing four hundred and fifty dollars a month, with CPU at two point one percent.
Now the Python code that automates this scan.
It begins by defining a list called assets.
Each entry is a tuple of three values: the instance identifier, the monthly cost, and the CPU percentage.

The four tuples match the table exactly: i-0a1b2c with four hundred and fifty and eighty-five point zero; i-9x8y7z with nine hundred and four point five; i-5m6n7o with fifteen hundred and sixty point zero; and i-1q2w3e with four hundred and fifty and two point one.
Next comes a function called scan.
It takes the assets and a threshold, which defaults to ten.
Inside, a list comprehension builds the candidates: every asset whose third element, the CPU value, is less than the threshold.
Then it computes monthly, the sum of the second element, the cost, across those candidates.
The function returns three things: the candidates, the monthly total, and that monthly total multiplied by twelve, which is the annual figure.
The script then prints the result of scanning all the assets.
After that, it builds a list called remaining, which contains every asset except the one whose identifier is i-9x8y7z.
In other words, it models removing that nine-hundred-dollar instance.
It then prints the scan of that remaining list.
Now the numbers.
The initial total monthly spend is three thousand three hundred dollars.
Two instances are candidates, and together they cost one thousand three hundred and fifty dollars monthly.
That is sixteen thousand two hundred dollars annually, if both can be eliminated without replacement costs.
If we remove the nine-hundred-dollar candidate, monthly spend falls to two thousand four hundred dollars.
That leaves four hundred and fifty dollars of monthly potential savings, which is five thousand four hundred dollars annually.
The initial potential reduction is one thousand three hundred and fifty divided by three thousand three hundred, which is approximately forty point nine one percent.
Finally, an important caution.
CPU alone does not prove waste.
Standby systems, memory-intensive workloads, seasonal services, and latency-sensitive applications may all have low average CPU.
So before acting, inspect memory, network activity, peak usage, dependencies, ownership, and recovery requirements.
Remember also how savings are calculated.
Rightsizing savings equal the old cost minus the replacement cost.
Termination savings may be reduced by contractual commitments and migration expenses.
In short, the script estimates opportunities, not realised return on investment.
